KEY MESSAGE 1... 

Increased cloud cover has occurred from forced ascent in the right 
entrance region to the south of an upper jet, as a stronger wave 
swings through Quebec en route to New England. The west-northest 
flow aloft itself contains additional weak waves, yet there is also 
surface high pressure. So while there are attempted scattered 
showers, initial ones have had to battle a lot of dry air in the 
boundary layer. As the surface high shifts to our east, a light 
return flow and pooling moisture within a developing frontal zone 
will generate waves of scattered light showers tonight into Monday 
morning. This will squeeze more towards the western Twin Tiers to 
Wyoming Valley PA tonight-early Monday as high pressure gets a 
temporary hold over Central NY-Catskills, but that zone will then 
drift across the rest of the region Monday afternoon. 

Any rain through Monday morning will be scattered and of little 
consequence. While that will remain mostly the case Monday afternoon 
through night, there will be more caveats. The developing frontal 
zone will see pooling moisture with precipitable water values 
reaching between 1.75-2.00 inches. Also, small amounts of 
instability aloft could result in isolated non-severe embedded 
thunder and thus more enhanced rates but that will be the exception 
not the rule. Most of the area will be just fine with a mostly 
cloudy seasonal day wand highs in the 70s to near 80 for the last 
day of August, with average rain amounts of only around a tenth of 
an inch or less. However, with the atmospheric profile trending more 
moist-adiabatic Monday afternoon through night, a narrow stripe or 
two of locally heavier rain cannot be totally ruled out if heavier 
showers can train over the same area. Meanwhile, there will be 
enough moisture around for typical areas of fog where breaks in 
clouds occur tonight-early Monday morning or Monday night.

KEY MESSAGE 2... 

A ring-of-fire scenario is appearing to take shape for Tuesday 
through Wednesday, and perhaps into Thursday for at least part of 
the area. That is a setup when there is a hot dome located to our 
southwest, with a belt of westerlies over the top of the dome, 
sending potential multiple waves of strong convection dropping 
through our region. The Storm Prediction Center continues to 
highlight Slight Risk of Severe Thunderstorms/15 percent chance 
within 25 miles of a point for at least portions of our area Tuesday-
Wednesday, and pressing south Thursday yet still possibly 
encroaching Northeast PA.

Warm and humid conditions at the surface will be coupled 
with brisk flow aloft and steepening midlevel lapse rates as any 
waves pass. Though the details have yet to shake out, convective 
parameters are favorable for there to be passing batches of strong 
to severe thunderstorms in our region, especially when and if waves 
coincide with peak diurnal heating each afternoon-evening. 
Convective Available Potential Energy (CAPE) probabilities have 
trended to 60-80 percent change of exceeding 1500 J/Kg for Tuesday 
afternoon and still 50-60 percent by Wednesday, especially west of I-
81. Top-heavy appearance of CAPE profiles in model soundings point 
to a large hail and wet microburst potential, with significant speed 
shear of 30-50 knots in the in 3-6km layer allowing for storm 
organization. This setup could even linger into Thursday for 
Northeast PA, though the primary belt of potential will be shifting 
south in response to more pronounced upper troughing across the 
northeast.

As with any setup that features multiple batches of storms in a warm 
and humid environment, each passing wave will pose an increase risk 
for excessive rainfall. Localized flash flooding thus cannot be 
ruled out through the midweek period, but details for where will not 
be apparent until we see where the initial zones of heavier batches 
of rain occur. As for the warmth, heat index values are likely to 
peak around 90 degrees Tuesday-Wednesday at lower elevations; not 
high enough for an Advisory but still very noticeable and perhaps 
impactful for anyone spending long periods outdoors without keeping 
up on hydration. Wyoming Valley PA could even push into lower-mid 
90s for heat index both afternoons. That should trend a bit lower 
by Thursday.

A broad upper trough pattern should lead to milder more seasonal 
early September temperatures Friday onward, with limited moisture 
and thus probably dry most of the time. National Blend of Models has 
daily Probability of Precipitation peaking only in the 15-30 percent 
range each day through next weekend.
